doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Symphony exclusion, redevelopment and the lost Fillmore clubs
summary: Elaine Jones's treatment, redevelopment wiping out Fillmore clubs, and his own luck with long engagements.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: lady, she had gone to Juilliard, she had played all over Europe, and she played in the symphony, so they wouldn’t let her — the probationary period. So Kurt Adler from the opera orchestra, he took her into the opera orchestra. So she played in the opera orchestra for years. And she went somewhere, I don’t know where she went, whether she went back East or whether she went over to Europe. But she was a fine tympanist. But see tympani players, that’s a high paid job in percussion because you have all the doubles. See you play all these doubles and each double means a little more money. So anyhow it’s hard to tell because we also — see when the redevelopment came along we lost a lot of our black clubs. The employment that we had in the black establishments. The cabarets, night clubs. There was one time out in the Fillmore where you had a place called the Scene, you had Blackshear’s Cafe Society, The Favorite Club, the Booker T. Washington Hotel, the California Theater Club, the Plantation, the New Orleans Swing Club, which later became the Champagne Supper Club, the Booker T. Washington Hotel, the Blue Mirror, the Ebony Plaza, then you had Bop City, the after hours spot, Jackson’s Nook after hours, another place on McAlister after hours, I don’t know what the name of it was but I went in there one night and Wes Montgomery was in there with his group. Then see the redevelopment, they destroyed all those. They just wiped them out. So we lost that employment see, and that was primarily black. Every now and then they’d have a mixed band. So I’ve been lucky see I can’t complain. Because I’ve been very lucky. I worked with Scobey, I worked with Hines, and then the different groups I worked with, a lot of engagements were long term engagements. Here the one I’m on now at Scott’s Seafood Restaurant at Jack London Square in Oakland, I’ve been on that job for Sunday mornings since 1986. And from that we get casuals — weddings and banquets and birthdays and all sorts — retirements, you name it see. So for me I’ve been lucky but some of our musicians weren’t so lucky. See because you have some that specialize, you know specialize in certain type of music. That’s why I say I’m lucky because I’ve been able to adapt to whatever the occasion calls for.
